Selected actions are encoded with dedicated query and candidate context tokens, and candidate-aware early fusion injects the candidate into every history token.
AI.result: Offline ablations show that dual retrieval improves major ranking metrics relative to the production baseline. In an online A/B test on sponsored-product search traffic, the model increased CTR, attributed conversion rate and orders per impression.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning long-term history retrieval on both query and candidate is a practical improvement for sponsored-product ranking in production search.

title: Breaking the $\sqrt{d}$ Communication Barrier in Federated Sampling with Adaptive Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
summary: This work proposes the Adaptive Federated Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (AFHMC) for Bayesian federated learning (FL) tasks. The prior work on HMC applications for FL achieves $O(\sqrt{d}/\epsilon)$ communication cost under log-convex distributions, already demonstrating its advantage over the Langevin dynamic-based counterpart. Based on a refined analysis, this paper further reveals the benefit of HMC for the FL regime by incorporating a control mechanism for local node shifts. We prove that AFHMC at most requires $O(\{d/\epsilon^2\}^{1/3})$ communication cost up to a logarithmic term, which is significantly better than the existing results. Moreover, the proposed method adapts to client heterogeneity. Under low-heterogeneity settings (i.e., the target sampling precision $\epsilon^2$ is higher than the heterogeneity level), the communication rate of AFHMC can be as good as $O(\log(d/\epsilon^2))$, resembling the communication costs for FL optimization tools. To the best of our knowledge, this provides the first logarithmic communication complexity result for federated sampling, even though it requires low heterogeneity. Numerically, we also justify AFHMC's advantage under the low-heterogeneity regime. Our code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Adaptive Federated Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (AFHMC) for Bayesian federated learning, with a communication cost that improves on prior HMC and Langevin-based results. Under low heterogeneity, the authors claim the first logarithmic communication complexity for federated sampling.
AI.motivation: Prior HMC work for federated learning achieves O(sqrt(d)/epsilon) communication cost under log-convex distributions, and the regime with heterogeneous clients needs better communication efficiency.
AI.method: AFHMC adds a control mechanism for local node shifts to federated HMC, which refines the analysis and adapts to client heterogeneity.
AI.result: The authors prove AFHMC requires at most O({d/epsilon^2}^(1/3)) communication cost up to a logarithmic term. Under low heterogeneity, where the target precision epsilon^2 exceeds the heterogeneity level, the communication rate can be O(log(d/epsilon^2)). Numerical experiments justify the advantage in the low-heterogeneity regime.
AI.conclusion: The results show HMC can achieve substantially lower communication cost than existing federated sampling methods, with logarithmic complexity possible when client heterogeneity is low.

title: Beyond Prediction Residuals: Conformal Regret Calibration for Robust Contextual Linear Optimization
summary: Predict-then-optimize systems convert contextual forecasts into decisions, yet conformal robust optimization typically calibrates prediction residuals rather than downstream loss. For linear optimization, this parameter-space geometry can be badly misaligned with decision risk: large objective perturbations may preserve the optimizer, while small boundary-crossing perturbations may cause substantial regret. We introduce Conformal Regret Sets, a post-hoc, model-agnostic framework that conformalizes an optimization-derived regret surrogate and uses its calibrated level set for minimax-regret refinement. We first show that directly conformalizing exact regret, although sufficient to certify the nominal predict-then-optimize decision, yields a degenerate robust problem: absent an exogenous bounded support, every alternative decision has unbounded worst-case regret. We therefore use SPO+, a pointwise upper bound on exact regret, as the conformal score, obtaining distribution-free finite-sample marginal regret guarantees under exchangeability. For contextual linear programs, the resulting set decomposes into polyhedral pieces aligned with the normal fan of the feasible polytope. A vertex is active if and only if its predicted suboptimality gap is at most half the calibrated threshold $\eta$, enabling local, output-sensitive generation of all relevant pieces. Moreover, if $\Gamma$ is the predicted gap to the closest competing vertex, the nominal and refined decisions admit the sharper worst-case-regret certificate $(\eta-2\Gamma)_+$, with an exact early exit when $\eta\leq 2\Gamma$. Experiments on contextual fractional knapsack validate the geometry and certificates: continuous refinement reduces the $0.95$-quantile and $\operatorname{CVaR}_{0.95}$ of regret by $9.1\%$ and $13.1\%$ relative to nominal PTO, while vertex-restricted refinement changes only $10.0\%$ of nominal decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Conformal Regret Sets, a post-hoc, model-agnostic method that conformalises a regret surrogate (SPO+) to refine predict-then-optimise decisions in contextual linear optimisation. On contextual fractional knapsack, it reduces the 0.95-quantile and CVaR_0.95 of regret by 9.1% and 13.1% relative to nominal predict-then-optimise.
AI.motivation: Conformal robust optimisation calibrates prediction residuals rather than downstream loss, which can be badly misaligned with decision risk in linear optimisation. Directly conformalising exact regret gives a degenerate robust problem with unbounded worst-case regret.
AI.method: SPO+, a pointwise upper bound on exact regret, is used as the conformal score, giving distribution-free finite-sample marginal regret guarantees under exchangeability. The resulting set decomposes into polyhedral pieces aligned with the normal fan of the feasible polytope, and a vertex is active if its predicted suboptimality gap is at most half the calibrated threshold.
AI.result: On contextual fractional knapsack, continuous refinement reduces the 0.95-quantile and CVaR_0.95 of regret by 9.1% and 13.1% relative to nominal predict-then-optimise, while vertex-restricted refinement changes only 10.0% of nominal decisions. The paper also gives a sharper worst-case regret certificate (eta - 2Gamma)_+.
AI.conclusion: Calibrating a regret surrogate rather than prediction residuals gives robust decisions with finite-sample guarantees and output-sensitive computation of the relevant decision pieces.

title: Trajectory Density Ratios under Weak Support: A Survey across the Sciences
summary: Many problems across the sciences compare two stochastic processes through the sequences they generate. Reinforcement learning asks what a new policy would return from the trajectories of an old one; molecular simulation asks how much more a ligand binds from samples of the unbound state; climate attribution asks how a heat wave shifted under warming; and language-model post-training asks what a deployed agent will do from logged interactions. In every case, one quantity would answer all these questions at once: the ratio of the two probability laws over their generated sequences, the trajectory density ratio. This ratio exists only under strong conditions. When one process reaches states the other cannot, the ratio does not exist; when their overlap is thin, its variance grows without control with the sequence length; and when they concentrate on different lower-dimensional sets, the ratio is undefined altogether. Weak support of this kind is the norm for sequence data, not a sampling accident, and its price is paid in identifiability rather than in noise alone. This survey organizes the field around a three-level diagnosis of weak support and a map of the nine retreats that methods take when the full ratio is out of reach, from direct estimation and reweighting through staged decomposition, stationarization, and partial-identification bounds to smoothing, transport couplings, operator spectra, and direct estimation of a single functional. Each retreat keeps part of what the ratio offers and pays for the rest, and each application domain has standardized the retreat its data force. The survey closes with open problems: testable diagnostics at every level, partial identification at the trajectory level, a rate theory of time-amplified error, and benchmarks with ground truth.

AI.tldr: The survey organises work on comparing two stochastic processes through the ratio of their trajectory distributions, the trajectory density ratio, which often fails to exist under weak support. It maps nine retreats that methods use when the full ratio is out of reach.
AI.motivation: Many scientific problems compare trajectories from two processes, but the trajectory density ratio exists only under strong overlap conditions. Weak support is the norm for sequence data, and its cost is identifiability rather than noise alone.
AI.method: The survey offers a three-level diagnosis of weak support and classifies nine retreats, including direct estimation, reweighting, staged decomposition, stationarisation, partial-identification bounds, smoothing, transport couplings, operator spectra, and direct estimation of a single functional.
AI.result: The survey does not report experimental numbers. It shows that each retreat keeps part of what the ratio offers at some cost, and that each application domain has standardised the retreat its data force.
AI.conclusion: Open problems include testable diagnostics at every level, partial identification at the trajectory level, a rate theory of time-amplified error, and benchmarks with ground truth.

title: A Black-Box Reduction from Regret to Multi-Level Coverage
summary: Online Conformal Prediction (OCP) sequentially constructs prediction sets whose average empirical coverage converges to a target level over time, for arbitrary, potentially adversarial datasets. In the multi-level setting, prediction sets are produced at $d$ coverage levels at once. Prior work argued for the use of online gradient descent with isotonic projections, which produces sets nested across levels, but with a $\sqrt{d}$ dependence in the per-level coverage convergence rate. Here, we both generalize and improve prior work. First, we show that isotonic projections can be used for the construction of multi-level online conformal prediction sets from \emph{any} online learning algorithm (not just gradient descent). Then, through a black-box reduction, we show that the linearized regret of the online algorithm itself automatically gives control over both per-level coverage and distributional consistency of multi-level predictions via Fenchel duality. Finally, by using the Weighted Interval Score, a standard scoring rule for assessing multi-level interval forecasts, we prove that these projections reduce both the size of the sets and their under-coverage. We study two instantiations of our theory, $p$-norm Online Mirror Descent and coordinate-wise Universal Portfolio methods, both improving the dependence on the number of levels to $\sqrt{\log d}$ for the multi-level OCP problem. Experiments on several datasets show favorable performance compared to baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a black-box reduction showing that the linearised regret of any online learning algorithm controls multi-level online conformal prediction coverage. Using p-norm Online Mirror Descent and coordinate-wise Universal Portfolio methods, it improves the dependence on the number of levels from sqrt(d) to sqrt(log d).
AI.motivation: Prior multi-level online conformal prediction work used online gradient descent with isotonic projections, which gives nested sets but has a sqrt(d) dependence on the number of coverage levels in the per-level convergence rate.
AI.method: Isotonic projections are shown to work with any online learning algorithm, not just gradient descent. Through a black-box reduction and Fenchel duality, the linearised regret of the online algorithm controls per-level coverage and distributional consistency across levels.
AI.result: Using the Weighted Interval Score, the authors prove the projections reduce both the size of the sets and their under-coverage. Experiments on several datasets show favourable performance compared with baselines.
AI.conclusion: The regret of the underlying online learner determines multi-level coverage guarantees, and choosing algorithms such as p-norm Online Mirror Descent or Universal Portfolio improves the level dependence to sqrt(log d).

title: The balance between feature learning and collapse in dynamical systems-based generative models
summary: Over the past decade, a growing body of work has established that implicit biases in learning dynamics fundamentally shape the solutions found by neural networks, governing their learned features and generalisation performance. However, despite these strides in deep learning theory, far less is known about representation learning in generative models based on dynamical systems, from normalising flows to diffusion. Importantly, empirical evidence suggests that continuous-time generative models can be prone to mode collapse, yet a learning theory explaining such biases remains elusive. To address this, we use tools from dynamical systems and operator theory to express the gradient flow of a general class of stochastic differential equations as a composition of linear operators, allowing us to relate collapse to low-rank biases in generative models. In variational inference and flow-matching tasks, we show that this bias can manifest in two different mechanisms: i) where collapsed models are stable fixed points of the gradient flow, or ii) in sequential feature learning, where smaller modes take progressively longer to be learned, producing an effective collapse for a fixed training budget. Together these findings point to a trade-off between feature learning and collapse, suggesting an operator view as a step towards a unified framework for understanding the learning dynamics of dynamical systems-based generative models.

AI.tldr: The paper uses operator theory to show that the gradient flow of stochastic-differential-equation-based generative models can be expressed as a composition of linear operators, linking mode collapse to low-rank bias. It identifies two mechanisms through which this bias appears in variational inference and flow matching.
AI.motivation: Continuous-time generative models such as normalising flows and diffusion models can suffer mode collapse, yet a learning theory explaining the bias behind this collapse is lacking, unlike the understanding of implicit bias in standard deep learning.
AI.method: Tools from dynamical systems and operator theory express the gradient flow of a general class of stochastic differential equations as a composition of linear operators, which relates collapse to low-rank biases.
AI.result: In variational inference and flow-matching tasks, the bias manifests in two ways: collapsed models can be stable fixed points of the gradient flow, or smaller modes are learned progressively more slowly, producing effective collapse under a fixed training budget.
AI.conclusion: There is a trade-off between feature learning and collapse, and an operator view is proposed as a step towards a unified framework for the learning dynamics of dynamical-systems-based generative models.

title: Causal discovery from Bayesian symbolic regression
summary: Causal discovery from observational data is central to scientific reasoning, yet established constraint-based and score-based methods often recover only a Markov equivalence class and provide no signal in bivariate or strongly autocorrelated regimes typical in some areas of science. Here, we recast causal discovery as a Bayesian symbolic regression problem. Given a set of candidate parents for each target variable, the Bayesian symbolic regression samples closed-form expressions from a posterior over symbolic models. The fraction of sampled expressions in which each candidate variable appears defines a posterior inclusion probability that we use as the causal score. This replaces pointwise model selection by an ensemble of plausible mechanisms. We evaluate the method on coupled nonlinear bivariate dynamics, on the CauseMe benchmark suite spanning linear, chaotic, nonlinear, higher-dimensional and high-noise settings, and on a four-variable biogeoscience structural causal model under Gaussian, heavy-tailed and mixed-noise regimes. Our approach is competitive with, and often outperforms, specialized causal discovery algorithms. Additionally, the method returns closed-form mechanisms leading to explicit causality and interpretability.

AI.tldr: The paper recasts causal discovery as Bayesian symbolic regression, using the posterior inclusion probability of each candidate parent across sampled closed-form expressions as the causal score. It is competitive with, and often outperforms, specialised causal discovery algorithms on several benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Constraint-based and score-based causal discovery often recovers only a Markov equivalence class and gives no signal in bivariate or strongly autocorrelated settings.
AI.method: For each target variable with a set of candidate parents, Bayesian symbolic regression samples closed-form expressions from a posterior over symbolic models. The fraction of sampled expressions containing each candidate defines its posterior inclusion probability, which serves as the causal score.
AI.result: The method is evaluated on coupled nonlinear bivariate dynamics, the CauseMe benchmark suite (linear, chaotic, nonlinear, higher-dimensional and high-noise settings), and a four-variable biogeoscience structural causal model under Gaussian, heavy-tailed and mixed noise. It is competitive with and often outperforms specialised causal discovery algorithms.
AI.conclusion: The approach yields an ensemble of plausible mechanisms rather than a single selected model, and returns closed-form mechanisms that give explicit causal interpretability.

title: Prediction with Foundation Models under Deployment Budgets
summary: Foundation models can supply predictions for a downstream task that draw on knowledge from extensive pretraining, but they differ in task-specific accuracy and query cost. We develop a framework that improves prediction for the task under a budget on the average query cost per input, using training data to learn which models to query and how to combine their outputs with features available without querying. The first method queries the same models for every input; the second lets them vary across inputs and uses Q-learning to decide which model to query next and when to stop. For the first method, we show that several individually inaccurate outputs can jointly outperform the best single one. It attains the minimax rate when the regression function depends on the outputs only through models within the budget. Otherwise, any method within the budget can be forced to a slower rate, which the first method attains. For the second method, we show when varying the queried models across inputs strictly improves on querying the same models for every input, and bound its prediction risk and average cost in finite samples. In simulations and a multimodal laptop price application, both methods outperform existing methods.

AI.tldr: The paper develops methods that predict a downstream target under a budget on average query cost to foundation models, learning which models to query and how to combine their outputs with unqueried features. Both methods outperform existing approaches in simulations and a multimodal laptop price application.
AI.motivation: Foundation models supply task predictions with differing task-specific accuracy and query cost, and a practitioner needs to choose which models to query under a cost budget.
AI.method: The first method queries the same models for every input and combines their outputs with features available without querying. The second lets the queried models vary across inputs and uses Q-learning to decide which model to query next and when to stop.
AI.result: The first method attains the minimax rate when the regression function depends only on outputs from models within the budget, and several individually inaccurate outputs can jointly outperform the best single one. The second method's advantage over fixed querying is characterised, and its prediction risk and average cost are bounded in finite samples.
AI.conclusion: Under a deployment budget, combining several foundation model outputs and adaptively choosing which to query can improve prediction, with theoretical guarantees for both the fixed and adaptive strategies.

title: Hidden Tails: Certifying Tail-Risk Claims under Selective Labels
summary: Historical decisions determine which outcomes are observed, potentially concealing a predictor's largest errors. Even unlimited data from the same observation process can therefore leave population tail risk unresolved. Here we derive sharp bounds on conditional value-at-risk, the average loss in a specified upper tail, for binary outcomes and bounded losses. These bounds span exactly the risks compatible with the observations and a stated limit on how outcome odds differ between observed and hidden cases at the same covariate values. Under stated regularity conditions, calibrated statistical certificates cover these ranges simultaneously across candidate predictors, supporting risk limits and model comparisons while separating statistical uncertainty from persistent ambiguity. For a fixed predictor and loss threshold, we derive a minimum-cost allocation for reducing excess-loss ambiguity by prioritizing hidden outcomes according to ambiguity removed per unit cost. This allocation treats audited population contributions as known and retains the original sensitivity bounds separately for audited and still-hidden outcomes. In controlled masking experiments with known loan repayments, recovering about 16% of hidden labels removes a median 61% of estimated fixed-threshold ambiguity, compared with 16% for random recovery. These results connect population tail-risk claims to the available evidence and identify where additional outcomes can sharpen their assessment.

AI.tldr: The paper derives sharp bounds on conditional value-at-risk for binary outcomes when some outcomes are hidden by historical decisions, and gives calibrated certificates that cover these ranges across candidate predictors. In masking experiments, recovering about 16% of hidden labels removes a median 61% of estimated fixed-threshold ambiguity, compared with 16% for random recovery.
AI.motivation: Historical decisions determine which outcomes are observed, so a predictor's largest errors can be hidden, and even unlimited data from the same observation process can leave population tail risk unresolved.
AI.method: Sharp bounds on conditional value-at-risk are derived for binary outcomes and bounded losses under a stated limit on how outcome odds differ between observed and hidden cases at the same covariate values. A minimum-cost allocation prioritises hidden outcomes by the ambiguity removed per unit cost.
AI.result: In controlled masking experiments with known loan repayments, recovering about 16% of hidden labels removes a median 61% of estimated fixed-threshold ambiguity, compared with 16% for random recovery.
AI.conclusion: The bounds separate statistical uncertainty from persistent ambiguity due to selective labels, and they identify where additional outcome labels would most sharpen tail-risk assessment.

title: From Granger causality to causal structure in dynamical systems
summary: The idea of testing whether the past of one signal improves the prediction of another can be traced back to Wiener. It was Granger who formalized the concept. Granger causality has become one of the most widely used tools to infer directed interactions between the components of a system. The name however can be misleading: it detects predictive relations among the measured signals, not causal relations among the mechanisms that generate them. This article starts by reviewing recent advances in observation-space Granger analysis. It then follows a path to directed structure in latent dynamical models, and asks under which conditions that structure can be read causally.

AI.tldr: The article reviews observation-space Granger causality, which tests whether the past of one signal improves prediction of another, and asks when directed structure in latent dynamical models can be read causally. It stresses that Granger causality detects predictive relations rather than causal mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Granger causality is widely used to infer directed interactions, but its name can mislead because it captures predictive relations among measured signals rather than causal relations among the mechanisms that generate them.
AI.method: The article is a review. It first covers recent advances in observation-space Granger analysis and then follows a path to directed structure in latent dynamical models.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experimental results. It identifies the conditions under which latent directed structure can be read causally as the central question.
AI.conclusion: Reading directed structure in latent dynamical models causally requires explicit conditions beyond predictive relations among observed signals.

title: Selected-Risk Calibration for Feasibility at Returned Decisions
summary: When an optimization problem uses a surrogate constraint, a decision that is feasible for the surrogate need not be feasible for the true constraint. We propose Selected-Risk Calibration (SRC), a framework that calibrates a learned constraint against the optimizer's returned decisions for objectives drawn from a given distribution. SRC guarantees that, with probability at least $1-\delta$, every margin it certifies on held-out objectives has selected risk, the probability that the returned decision is infeasible, of at most $\gamma$. We also show that the random-input coverage guarantee of split conformal prediction does not bound the selected risk, and that likelihood-ratio reweighting for feedback covariate shift does not apply when the learned constraint is active at the returned decision. Our experiments show that a conformal margin covering about $90\%$ of random inputs covered as few as $17\%$ of the returned decisions, and every certified margin had a violation rate below its target on unseen objectives. Moreover, at equal cost, SRC's correction had fewer or equal infeasible solutions to the baselines in 57 of 62 comparisons. The SRC framework applies to any setting in which a surrogate model chooses a decision whose feasibility can be verified for a sample of instances.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Selected-Risk Calibration (SRC), which calibrates a learned surrogate constraint against the decisions an optimiser actually returns, with a probabilistic guarantee on the selected risk of infeasibility. Standard conformal margins covering about 90% of random inputs covered as few as 17% of returned decisions.
AI.motivation: When an optimisation problem uses a surrogate constraint, decisions feasible for the surrogate may be infeasible for the true constraint, and random-input coverage guarantees from split conformal prediction do not bound this selected risk.
AI.method: SRC calibrates the learned constraint against returned decisions for objectives drawn from a given distribution. It guarantees that, with probability at least 1 - delta, every certified margin has selected risk, the probability that the returned decision is infeasible, at most gamma. The authors also show that likelihood-ratio reweighting for feedback covariate shift does not apply when the learned constraint is active at the returned decision.
AI.result: A conformal margin covering about 90% of random inputs covered only 17% of the returned decisions in the experiments, and every certified margin had a violation rate below its target on unseen objectives. At equal cost, SRC's correction had fewer or equal infeasible solutions than the baselines in 57 of 62 comparisons.
AI.conclusion: SRC applies to any setting where a surrogate model chooses a decision whose feasibility can be verified on a sample of instances, and it targets the risk that matters for returned decisions rather than random inputs.

title: Lower-Level Agnostic Bilevel Optimization
summary: Bilevel optimization is a fundamental framework for machine learning problems, where an upper-level (UL) objective depends on the solution of a nested lower-level (LL) problem. Existing bilevel algorithms typically assume that the LL objective is available for evaluation, differentiation, or unrolling. However, this assumption can fail when the LL response is produced by a black-box solver, simulator, adversary, or learned predictor. In this paper, we study LL agnostic bilevel optimization, where the UL learner has access only to an approximate LL solution $\bar{\mathbf{y}}(\mathbf{x})$ and cannot query the LL objective, its gradients, Hessian/Jacobian information, or the procedure that generates the LL response. We propose LeGo-BiO, a coordinate-wise pseudo-hypergradient method that estimates the missing Jacobian $\nabla _{\mathbf{x}}\bar{\mathbf{y}}(\mathbf{x})$ using finite differences of $\bar{\mathbf{y}}(\cdot)$. For each UL coordinate, LeGo-BiO constructs a decision vector subject to 1-sparse updates, thereby isolating the corresponding Jacobian column needed in the UL gradient computation. This avoids the directional-projection limitation of full-parameter response differences and, unlike derivative-free/zeroth-order approximations of the entire UL gradient, preserves the available first-order gradient information with respect to the UL variables for more accurate UL gradient evaluation. We establish convergence guarantees for LeGo-BiO in both deterministic and stochastic settings under an LL error-bound/Polyak-Lojasiewicz-type condition, without requiring LL strong convexity. Our bounds yield an $O(T^{-1})$ rate in the deterministic setting and an $O(T^{-1/2})$ rate in the stochastic setting when the LL approximation error decreases geometrically. Experiments demonstrate competitive performance of LeGo-BiO despite being agnostic to the LL objective.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes LeGo-BiO, a bilevel optimisation method for lower-level agnostic settings, where the upper level only has an approximate lower-level solution and cannot query the lower-level objective or its derivatives. It estimates the missing Jacobian by coordinate-wise finite differences and reports competitive performance.
AI.motivation: Existing bilevel algorithms assume the lower-level objective can be evaluated, differentiated or unrolled, which fails when the lower-level response comes from a black-box solver, simulator, adversary or learned predictor.
AI.method: For each upper-level coordinate, LeGo-BiO constructs a decision vector with 1-sparse updates to isolate the corresponding column of the Jacobian of the lower-level solution, estimated by finite differences. This avoids the directional-projection limitation of full-parameter response differences and keeps first-order gradient information for the upper-level variables.
AI.result: Convergence guarantees are given in deterministic and stochastic settings under a lower-level error-bound or Polyak-Lojasiewicz-type condition without lower-level strong convexity. The rate is O(T^-1) in the deterministic setting and O(T^-1/2) in the stochastic setting when the lower-level approximation error decreases geometrically. Experiments show competitive performance.
AI.conclusion: Bilevel optimisation can be carried out without access to the lower-level objective, with convergence guarantees, at a performance level competitive with methods that require full lower-level access.

title: Match the Geometry Before the Surrogate: Extreme Low-Budget Optimization in High Dimensions
comment: NeurIPS 2026 (camera-ready). 10 pages of main text plus appendices and the NeurIPS paper checklist, 38 pages in total. Code and result files: this https URL . Project page: this https URL
summary: Low-budget molecular optimization is often framed as Bayesian optimization in a learned latent space, but standard benchmarks typically allow hundreds or thousands of evaluations, whereas a realistic wet-lab round may allow only a few dozen. We revisit this regime using a SELFIES molecular variational autoencoder (VAE) with a Gaussian prior and GuacaMol objectives at N = 30 evaluations. The main finding is not a new surrogate model, but an interaction in candidate generation. The encoder means of a reference set of molecules concentrate near a narrow spherical shell, while many high-dimensional optimizers propose candidates from boxes or box-shaped trust regions. We study a simple constraint, the on-sphere scaffold, that restricts candidate generation to this shell. We then introduce two minimal optimizers to probe what remains useful once the support is fixed. GeoWalk performs geodesic local search on the shell without a surrogate. After 30 evaluations, it shows no detected difference from a Gaussian-process (GP) surrogate on the shell, which is ahead earlier in the budget. GeoCMA adds covariance learning in a random subspace. It does not improve on GeoWalk in the molecular benchmark. On LassoBench it has a lower mean loss than GeoWalk, but full-dimensional CMA-ES remains stronger on most tasks. A factorial experiment with a single GP crosses the candidate support (shell or box) with the acquisition maximizer (a finite candidate set or a continuous optimizer). In this benchmark, shell candidates outperformed box candidates when acquisition was maximized over a candidate set, but not with continuous maximization by L-BFGS-B. These results come from a controlled study of one Gaussian-prior VAE benchmark and do not recommend VAEs for molecular optimization. The practical lesson is to control the candidate support and the acquisition maximizer before attributing a gain to the surrogate.

AI.tldr: In a 30-evaluation molecular optimisation setting with a SELFIES VAE, the paper finds that candidate support matters more than the surrogate: restricting candidates to the spherical shell where reference encodings concentrate gives the gain. Simple geodesic local search on the shell performs about as well as a GP surrogate.
AI.motivation: Low-budget molecular optimisation is often treated as Bayesian optimisation in a learned latent space, but benchmarks allow hundreds or thousands of evaluations, far more than a realistic wet-lab round of a few dozen.
AI.method: With a SELFIES molecular VAE using a Gaussian prior and GuacaMol objectives at N = 30 evaluations, the authors constrain candidate generation to the shell (on-sphere scaffold) and test two minimal optimisers. GeoWalk performs geodesic local search on the shell without a surrogate, and GeoCMA adds covariance learning in a random subspace. A factorial experiment crosses candidate support (shell or box) with the acquisition maximiser (candidate set or L-BFGS-B).
AI.result: After 30 evaluations, GeoWalk shows no detected difference from a GP surrogate on the shell. GeoCMA does not improve on GeoWalk on the molecular benchmark, though on LassoBench it has lower mean loss than GeoWalk, while full-dimensional CMA-ES remains stronger on most tasks. Shell candidates outperform box candidates when acquisition is maximised over a candidate set, but not with continuous L-BFGS-B maximisation.
AI.conclusion: Candidate support and the acquisition maximiser should be controlled before attributing gains to the surrogate. The results come from one Gaussian-prior VAE benchmark and do not recommend VAEs for molecular optimisation.

title: Objective Diversification of Dynamic Hedging
summary: A hedging objective reflects the risk preference of the hedger, so the conventional approach is to estimate the hedge ratio directly under the chosen objective. This paper asks whether that estimate should be used alone. We construct five objective-specific rolling hedge-ratio estimators---minimum variance, least absolute deviation (LAD), downside semivariance, lower-tail quantile, and Expected Shortfall (ES)---from the same historical stock--market returns, and combine the resulting estimates under a fixed final evaluation objective. Separate multi-output ExtraTrees models predict the within-stock-date ranks of the five candidates under MSE, LAD, downside semivariance, and 10\% quantile loss. The design uses pre-specified 60-, 90-, 120-, and 180-day windows with objective-matched rolling estimators as benchmarks. Adaptive weighting improves the corresponding loss in all sixteen objective--window comparisons. Equal weighting, which uses the same objective-specific hedge ratios without state variables or learned reweighting, already improves downside and quantile hedging. The results therefore suggest that estimates generated under other objectives can be useful even when the final hedging preference and evaluation objective are fixed, while adaptive weighting can provide a further improvement.

AI.tldr: The paper builds five objective-specific rolling hedge-ratio estimators and combines their estimates with adaptive weighting learned by ExtraTrees, which improves the targeted loss in all sixteen objective-window comparisons. Equal weighting of the same estimates already improves downside and quantile hedging.
AI.motivation: The conventional approach estimates a hedge ratio directly under the hedger's chosen objective, but it is unclear whether that single estimate should be used alone when the final objective is fixed.
AI.method: Five rolling hedge-ratio estimators are built from the same stock and market returns under minimum variance, least absolute deviation, downside semivariance, lower-tail quantile and Expected Shortfall objectives. Multi-output ExtraTrees models predict within-stock-date ranks of the five candidates under MSE, LAD, downside semivariance and 10% quantile losses, using pre-specified 60-, 90-, 120- and 180-day windows with objective-matched benchmarks.
AI.result: Adaptive weighting improves the corresponding loss in all sixteen objective-window comparisons. Equal weighting already improves downside and quantile hedging over the objective-matched benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Estimates generated under other objectives can be useful even when the final hedging preference and evaluation objective are fixed, and adaptive weighting can provide a further improvement.

title: On the universal structure in deterministic generative diffusion
summary: Diffusion-based generative modeling has emerged as a general computational framework for simulating high-dimensional, structured data across various domains. Understanding its generative mechanisms is paramount for advancing model training and inference in a principled way. Here, we demonstrate that deterministic sampling trajectories share a universal geometric structure invariant to data modalities and diffusion model implementations. This structure can be largely explained by an exactly solvable model based on the optimal linear denoiser.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that deterministic sampling trajectories of diffusion models share a universal geometric structure that is independent of data modality and model implementation. An exactly solvable model based on the optimal linear denoiser largely explains this structure.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models are a general framework for generating high-dimensional structured data, but their generative mechanisms are not well understood, which limits principled improvements to training and inference.
AI.method: The authors analyze deterministic sampling trajectories across diffusion models and data types to identify a shared geometric structure, then build an exactly solvable model based on the optimal linear denoiser to explain it.
AI.result: Deterministic trajectories are found to share a universal geometric structure, and the exactly solvable linear-denoiser model accounts for much of it.
AI.conclusion: The structure is a model- and modality-invariant property of diffusion sampling, offering a principled basis for understanding and improving diffusion training and inference.

title: Bias, Measurement Error, and Double-Dipping: When Can GNN Convolutions Help Brain Connectome Prediction?
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 32 pages, 9 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are an important tool for fMRI prediction, where empirical functional connectivity matrices serve both as features and for graph construction. However, recent studies and our own experiments show that these methods often fail to outperform simpler graph-agnostic baselines. We propose a statistical explanation for this failure by formulating connectome prediction as an errors-in-variables (EIV) problem: the true connectome is latent, while the observed covariance matrix is a noisy finite-time-series estimate. In a linear asymptotic setting, we decompose the effect of graph convolution into three mechanisms: smoothing-induced bias and variance reduction, graph estimation error, and a double-dipping effect arising when the same noisy matrix determines both graph and features. Under a latent community model adapted to neuroscience, we identify a narrow favorable regime, set by the brain community structure, the predictive signal, the graph construction and the recording length, in which message passing can improve prediction. Simulations validate this decomposition, while real-data experiments illustrate that connectome GNN pipelines often fall outside this regime. Our results provide a first step towards explaining when graph convolutions can help brain connectome prediction, and why they often do not.

AI.tldr: The paper explains why graph neural networks often fail to beat graph-agnostic baselines for fMRI connectome prediction, by framing the task as an errors-in-variables problem. It identifies a narrow regime in which graph convolution can help.
AI.motivation: Existing GNN methods for fMRI prediction often fail to outperform simpler graph-agnostic baselines, and no principled explanation for this failure had been given.
AI.method: The observed covariance matrix is modeled as a noisy estimate of a latent true connectome. In a linear asymptotic setting, the effect of graph convolution is decomposed into smoothing-induced bias and variance reduction, graph estimation error, and a double-dipping effect, analyzed under a latent community model adapted to neuroscience.
AI.result: Message passing can improve prediction only within a narrow favorable regime determined by brain community structure, predictive signal strength, graph construction and recording length. Simulations validate the decomposition, and real-data connectome GNN pipelines often fall outside this regime.
AI.conclusion: The results give a first explanation of when graph convolutions help connectome prediction and why they often do not, pointing to the need to account for estimation noise in graph construction.

title: SAMBoost: Spatially Aware Mesh Boosting
summary: We propose SAMBoost (Spatially Aware Mesh Boosting), a gradient boosting method that combines tree-based covariate modelling with a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) latent spatial field through a single penalised objective. At each boosting iteration, the predictor is decomposed into separate covariate and spatial components. The method is motivated by applications in which the spatial effect is not a nuisance to be removed but a quantity of interest that must be recovered alongside the covariates. In insurance, for example, practitioners need both flexible nonlinear covariate effects and an interpretable geographic risk surface that can be reported on its own. Existing approaches often involve trade-offs, offering flexible covariate modelling but no explicit spatial field, rigorous spatial inference with a fixed additive covariate structure, or a combination of both at computational costs that limit practicality for large datasets. SAMBoost addresses these goals within the boosting loop, and the underlying mesh produces a sparse precision structure whose cost is largely independent of sample size. On simulations and on an open benchmark, SAMBoost matches or improves on the predictive accuracy of joint Gaussian process and tree boosting approaches. It is also faster and recovers the spatial field and covariate effects more accurately. When covariate effects include interactions, it outperforms additive Bayesian spatial models. Applied to a flood insurance portfolio with 4.9 million records, SAMBoost trains on the full training set without subsampling and runs about sixteen times faster than a Bayesian reference, with a consistent spatial risk surface. A public Python implementation is available.

AI.tldr: SAMBoost is a gradient boosting method that jointly fits tree-based covariate effects and an SPDE-based latent spatial field through one penalised objective. It recovers an interpretable spatial risk surface alongside flexible covariate modelling.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches either model covariates flexibly without an explicit spatial field, offer rigorous spatial inference only with a fixed additive covariate structure, or combine both at computational costs that limit use on large datasets.
AI.method: At each boosting iteration the predictor is decomposed into separate covariate and spatial components. The spatial field is represented on a mesh whose sparse precision structure has a cost largely independent of sample size.
AI.result: On simulations and an open benchmark, SAMBoost matches or improves predictive accuracy relative to joint Gaussian process and tree boosting approaches, is faster, and recovers spatial and covariate effects more accurately. With interactions it outperforms additive Bayesian spatial models. On a flood insurance portfolio of 4.9 million records it trains on the full data without subsampling and runs about sixteen times faster than a Bayesian reference.
AI.conclusion: SAMBoost makes it practical to recover an explicit spatial risk surface together with flexible covariate effects at large scale, which matters for insurance pricing and similar applications; a public Python implementation is available.

title: Causal Discovery Grounding and the Naturalness Assumption
summary: Standard causal discovery postulates that structure can be described by a directed acyclic graph (DAG), which can be partially reconstructed by using the faithfulness principle. According to this principle, conditional independencies in the observational distribution correspond exactly to those encoded in the unknown DAG. However, such algorithms are challenged by the fact that, without even stronger assumptions, approximate failures of faithfulness are empirically undistinguishable from exact ones. This leaves an inferential gap which can lead to major implications to causal effect identification. We introduce a different perspective, not reliant on exact independencies. By considering the specialized problem of discovering whether unmeasured confounding can be ruled out for a particular cause-effect pair, we introduce a principle we call naturalness, in which the strength of observational associations bounds the strength of causal dependencies. The bounding function is unknown, with degrees of freedom not present in faithfulness. We model uncertainty about this function using a Bayesian framing which allows for the use of experiments from separate studies, grounding an adaptive causal discovery principle on historical experimental data. We demonstrate its usefulness in partial identification of causal effects, and discuss how the promising results can motivate new principles for general causal discovery.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes naturalness, a principle in which the strength of observational associations bounds the strength of causal dependencies, as an alternative to faithfulness for ruling out unmeasured confounding. It uses Bayesian modelling with historical experiments to ground causal discovery and partial identification of effects.
AI.motivation: Standard causal discovery relies on faithfulness, but approximate faithfulness failures cannot be distinguished empirically from exact ones, creating an inferential gap that affects causal effect identification.
AI.method: For a specific cause-effect pair, the method asks whether unmeasured confounding can be ruled out by bounding causal dependence with observational association through an unknown bounding function. Uncertainty about this function is modelled in a Bayesian framework that incorporates experiments from separate studies.
AI.result: The principle yields promising partial identification of causal effects in the demonstrations reported.
AI.conclusion: Naturalness offers a new perspective that may motivate further principles for general causal discovery beyond exact independence assumptions.

title: Zeroth-Order Langevin Dynamics for Stochastic Nonconvex Optimization: Curvature Regularization and Non-Asymptotic Guarantees
summary: Zeroth-order methods provide a way to optimize stochastic nonconvex objectives using only noisy function evaluations. However, the smoothing inherent in their gradient estimators effectively modifies the objective being optimized. In particular, Gaussian smoothing with smoothing parameter $\eta>0$ induces, to leading order, an implicit Hessian-trace regularization, which motivates the study of the curvature-regularized objective of the form $f(x)+(\eta^2/2) tr(\nabla^2 f(x))$. We develop a non-asymptotic theory in the nonconvex setting for a class of algorithms called stochastic zeroth-order Langevin dynamics (ZOLD), which use only noisy function evaluations and do not have access to first- or higher-order derivative information, and derive excess-risk guarantees for the curvature-regularized objective. We first control the finite-time distribution of the ZOLD iterates in Wasserstein distance with respect to the Gibbs measure associated with the Gaussian-smoothed objective. An explicit coupling between the smoothing and inverse temperature parameters then quantifies the proximity of this measure to the Gibbs measure associated with the corresponding Hessian-trace-regularized objective. These distributional estimates in Wasserstein distance lead to excess-risk bounds for the curvature-regularized objective. Our analysis accommodates assumptions under which the stochastic function evaluations are allowed to have non-uniform dependence on the data stream. In addition, the constants in the non-asymptotic bounds do not rely on log-Sobolev or Poincaré inequalities as in prior zeroth-order Langevin analyses. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first non-asymptotic analysis of a zeroth-order Langevin method that simultaneously establishes excess-risk guarantees for a curvature-regularized objective and Wasserstein guarantees for the associated Gibbs measure in the nonconvex setting.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes stochastic zeroth-order Langevin dynamics for nonconvex optimization and shows that Gaussian smoothing implicitly optimizes a curvature-regularized objective. It gives non-asymptotic excess-risk and Wasserstein guarantees for this objective.
AI.motivation: Zeroth-order methods modify the objective through gradient smoothing, and prior zeroth-order Langevin analyses relied on log-Sobolev or Poincare inequalities for their constants.
AI.method: Gaussian smoothing with parameter eta induces an implicit Hessian-trace regularization, giving the objective f(x) + (eta^2/2) tr(Hessian of f(x)). The analysis controls the finite-time distribution of ZOLD iterates in Wasserstein distance relative to the Gibbs measure of the smoothed objective, then couples smoothing and inverse temperature to compare with the curvature-regularized Gibbs measure. The analysis allows non-uniform dependence of the stochastic evaluations on the data stream.
AI.result: The paper derives excess-risk bounds for the curvature-regularized objective and Wasserstein guarantees for the associated Gibbs measure, with constants that do not depend on log-Sobolev or Poincare inequalities.
AI.conclusion: This is claimed to be the first non-asymptotic analysis of a zeroth-order Langevin method that yields both excess-risk and Wasserstein guarantees in the nonconvex setting.

title: Close and Sort: Exact Maximum-Likelihood Aggregation of Cyclic Rank-Two Preferences
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at the 20th ACM International Conference on Web Search and Data Mining (WSDM 2027). Code: this https URL
summary: Pairwise probabilities arise in rank aggregation, recommendation, and human or LLM evaluation, yet converting them into a maximum-likelihood list is a weighted Kemeny problem and is NP-hard in general. Known exact algorithms for rank-two tournaments use only comparison signs and do not optimize this likelihood. We show that the weighted problem is exactly solvable when the skew-symmetric log-odds matrix $W_{ij}=\log(p_{ij}/p_{ji})$ has rank two, including when the induced preferences contain cycles. Writing $W_{ij}=\det(h_i,h_j)$ and adding the closing vector $h_0=-\sum_i h_i$ turns the objective into twice the signed area of a closed polygon. This geometry yields CloseSort, which polar-sorts the $n+1$ edge vectors, cuts after $h_0$, and returns a global maximum-likelihood order in $O(n\log n)$ time from the factors. The same geometry identifies the runner-up and gives a stability certificate beyond exact rank two. When the smallest determinant $\delta$ of two consecutive edges in the closed angular cycle is positive, it is exactly the best-to-runner-up log-likelihood gap. For $W=W_0+E$, the CloseSort order of $W_0$ has regret at most $\sum_{i<j}|E_{ij}|$ on $W$ and remains optimal whenever this sum is below $\delta$, a worst-case tight threshold. In 5,120 determinant-logit simulations, increasing the observations per pair from 4 to 64 raises the fraction on which rank-two projection outperforms the empirical plug-in optimum from 68.6% to 85.7%. On 3,600 Arena-Hard LLM-judge profiles drawn from 63 systems and ten judges, the leading rank-two component captures 89.2% of the log-odds energy. On profiles containing a directed majority triangle, CloseSort reduces normalized regret by 44% relative to Borda and improves the mean normalized objective over each of eight baselines. With factors supplied, it is 8,407 times faster than exact dynamic programming on 18-item rankings.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the weighted Kemeny aggregation problem is exactly solvable when the skew-symmetric log-odds matrix has rank two, even with cyclic preferences. The resulting CloseSort algorithm returns a global maximum-likelihood order in O(n log n) time.
AI.motivation: Converting pairwise probabilities into a maximum-likelihood ranking is NP-hard in general, and known exact algorithms for rank-two tournaments use only comparison signs and do not optimize the likelihood.
AI.method: Writing the log-odds as a determinant and adding a closing vector turns the objective into twice the signed area of a closed polygon. CloseSort polar-sorts the n+1 edge vectors and cuts after the closing vector. The geometry also identifies the runner-up and gives a stability certificate, and a regret bound is given for perturbed matrices.
AI.result: In 5,120 simulations, raising observations per pair from 4 to 64 increased the fraction of cases where rank-two projection beats the empirical plug-in optimum from 68.6% to 85.7%. On 3,600 Arena-Hard LLM-judge profiles, the leading rank-two component captures 89.2% of the log-odds energy. On profiles with a directed majority triangle, CloseSort reduces normalized regret by 44% relative to Borda, and it is 8,407 times faster than exact dynamic programming on 18-item rankings when factors are supplied.
AI.conclusion: The geometric view gives exact and fast maximum-likelihood aggregation for near rank-two preference data, including cyclic preferences that sign-based methods cannot handle optimally.

title: Confronting Uncertainty in Mechanism-AI Coupled Dynamical Systems via Optimal Transport and Information Geometry: Part I. Distribution Learning
summary: Mechanism-AI coupled dynamical systems are increasingly used to study complex biological systems. However, uncertainty associated with noisy, sparse, and partially observed data limits their reliability. This paper presents a systematic mathematical formulation for treating these uncertainties from the perspective of optimal transport and information geometry. We formulate the uncertainty quantification problem as the minimization of an energy functional on a probability density space equipped with a Riemannian metric, with the loss evaluated through a differential equation, and give a unified description of the gradient flows of the energy functional under specific metrics, such as the Wasserstein and Fisher-Rao metrics. Furthermore, we present corresponding numerical methods for solving these gradient flows using abstract adjoint sensitivity analysis. The formulation connects a range of Bayesian inference methods for dynamical systems; numerical experiments compare posterior approximation and predictive uncertainty under a common computational budget. Moreover, it also provides a geometric perspective on dynamical modeling and the study of heterogeneity evolution.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates uncertainty quantification for mechanism-AI coupled dynamical systems as minimizing an energy functional over a Riemannian space of probability densities. It unifies Wasserstein and Fisher-Rao gradient flows with adjoint-based numerical methods and connects several Bayesian inference approaches for dynamical systems.
AI.motivation: Noisy, sparse and partially observed data limit the reliability of mechanism-AI coupled models of biological systems, and a systematic treatment of this uncertainty is needed.
AI.method: Uncertainty quantification is posed as minimizing an energy functional on a probability density space with a Riemannian metric, with the loss evaluated through a differential equation. Gradient flows under Wasserstein and Fisher-Rao metrics are described in a unified way, and they are solved numerically using abstract adjoint sensitivity analysis.
AI.result: Numerical experiments compare posterior approximation and predictive uncertainty of the connected Bayesian methods under a common computational budget.
AI.conclusion: The formulation gives a geometric perspective on dynamical modeling and on the study of heterogeneity evolution. This is Part I and focuses on distribution learning.

title: A Geometric Theory for Nonequilibrium Transformer Dynamics
comment: 29 pages Submitted to Proc Roy Soc A
summary: We develop a variational and geometric theory based on statistical physics for the joint evolution of Transformer attention and token representations at fixed model parameters. To this end, we introduce a free energy for the attention and model the evolution of the attention weights by its Fisher--Rao gradient flow. At fixed token representations, we prove that the softmax matrix is the unique free-energy minimiser and that every positive attention trajectory converges to it. For prescribed time-dependent representations, we show that the attention dynamics becomes linear after a change to logit variables. This result yields tracking bounds relative to the instantaneous softmax and sufficient conditions for attention to converge to a fixed matrix. Hamiltonian dynamics for the representations and their momenta are then coupled to the attention relaxation driven by the same energy. This coupling results in an energy-dissipation law. We also develop two alternative Hamiltonians incorporating the attention value map. We prove global well-posedness of the attention flow and all three coupled systems.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a statistical-physics variational theory of Transformer attention with a free energy and Fisher-Rao gradient flow. It proves that the softmax matrix is the unique free-energy minimiser, and it couples attention dynamics with Hamiltonian dynamics for token representations.
AI.motivation: The paper studies how attention weights and token representations evolve jointly at fixed parameters, which standard analyses of the softmax attention map do not capture as a dynamical system.
AI.method: A free energy for attention is introduced, and attention evolves by its Fisher-Rao gradient flow. For fixed representations, attention is analyzed directly. For prescribed time-dependent representations, a change to logit variables makes the dynamics linear. Hamiltonian dynamics for representations and momenta is coupled to attention relaxation through the same energy, and two alternative Hamiltonians incorporate the value map.
AI.result: The authors prove that the softmax matrix is the unique free-energy minimiser, that every positive attention trajectory converges to it, and that the coupled system obeys an energy-dissipation law. They also give tracking bounds relative to the instantaneous softmax, sufficient conditions for convergence to a fixed matrix, and global well-posedness of the flows.
AI.conclusion: The theory offers a variational and geometric account of joint attention and representation dynamics in Transformers, with rigorous convergence and well-posedness guarantees.

title: Robust Satisficing Ensemble: Scalable Model Aggregation Under Distribution Shifts
summary: Standard ensemble methods can improve robustness by mitigating individual model stochasticity, but they frequently fail to generalize beyond the training distribution, leaving systems vulnerable to out-of-distribution (OOD) data. We introduce the Robust Satisficing Ensemble (RSE), a scalable probabilistic aggregation framework designed to secure model combinations by minimizing their fragility against distributional changes. By bridging a robust satisficing objective with a quadratic risk surrogate, RSE derives an analytical inner adversary. This fundamental reformulation enables highly efficient weight updates without the computational bottleneck of standard minimax optimization, crucially decoupling optimization complexity from sample size to scale effectively to large datasets. In particular, we prove a geometrically decaying truncation error for the fragility approximation via Lagrange-Burmann expansion and establish stationarity guarantees for RSE. We evaluate RSE across a comprehensive spectrum of distribution shifts, including adversarial label shift (SST-5, TREC), natural subpopulation and temporal shifts (CivilComments, HuffPost). Our results demonstrate that RSE consistently outperforms strong robust baselines, including GroupDRO, IRM, and SRM. These findings establish RSE as a practical, theoretically grounded safeguard for reliable model aggregation in dynamic environments.

AI.tldr: Robust Satisficing Ensemble (RSE) is a scalable probabilistic aggregation method that combines models by minimizing their fragility under distribution shift. It avoids costly minimax optimization by deriving an analytical inner adversary.
AI.motivation: Standard ensembles do not generalize beyond the training distribution and remain vulnerable to out-of-distribution data.
AI.method: RSE bridges a robust satisficing objective with a quadratic risk surrogate, which yields an analytical inner adversary and allows efficient weight updates whose complexity is decoupled from sample size. The fragility approximation is controlled through a Lagrange-Burmann expansion.
AI.result: RSE consistently outperforms GroupDRO, IRM and SRM on adversarial label shift (SST-5, TREC) and natural subpopulation and temporal shifts (CivilComments, HuffPost). The paper proves a geometrically decaying truncation error for the fragility approximation and establishes stationarity guarantees.
AI.conclusion: RSE is presented as a practical and theoretically grounded way to aggregate models reliably in dynamic environments with distribution shift.

title: Prescriptive Learning of Linear Policies with Feasibility Guarantees for Binary Decision-Making
summary: Binary decision-making under uncertainty arises across a wide range of applications, including energy systems scheduling, transportation, and workforce planning. While machine learning has been increasingly applied to accelerate or replace mixed-integer solvers in such settings, existing approaches rely on predictive learning, training models to reproduce optimal decisions from labeled data, which lacks knowledge of counterfactual outcomes and provides no guarantees that the resulting decisions will be feasible. This limitation is further compounded under distributional shift, where policies trained on historical data may produce systematically infeasible decisions. We propose a prescriptive learning framework for binary decision-making that addresses both limitations. Rather than predicting optimal labels, the framework jointly optimizes over linear decision policies and feasible assignments across all training scenarios, allowing feasible alternatives and their operational performance to be considered directly during training. We further extend the framework to a distributionally robust chance-constrained formulation using a Wasserstein ambiguity set, which enforces feasibility with a prescribed probability under the worst-case distribution in the ambiguity set and enables a tunable trade-off between robustness and solution quality. We demonstrate the framework on two case studies, namely a unit commitment problem and a staff allocation problem. Out-of-sample experiments under test distributions that either match or differ from the training distribution show that the robust model is more conservative when the two distributions coincide, while under distributional shift it substantially reduces unmet demand and lowers total cost by up to 76.5% relative to classical predictive learning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a prescriptive learning framework that jointly optimizes linear policies and feasible binary assignments, instead of predicting optimal labels. A distributionally robust chance-constrained extension gives feasibility guarantees under a Wasserstein ambiguity set.
AI.motivation: Predictive learning for binary decisions reproduces optimal labels without counterfactual knowledge and gives no feasibility guarantees, and policies trained on historical data can become systematically infeasible under distribution shift.
AI.method: The framework optimizes linear decision policies and feasible assignments across all training scenarios, so feasible alternatives and their performance enter training. It is extended to a distributionally robust chance-constrained formulation with a Wasserstein ambiguity set, which enforces feasibility with a prescribed probability under the worst-case distribution and gives a tunable trade-off between robustness and solution quality.
AI.result: On a unit commitment problem and a staff allocation problem, the robust model is more conservative when test and training distributions coincide. Under distribution shift it substantially reduces unmet demand and lowers total cost by up to 76.5% relative to classical predictive learning.
AI.conclusion: Prescriptive learning with robust feasibility constraints can give decisions that remain feasible and cost-effective under shift, unlike predictive approaches.

title: Causal Outcome Learning with Noisy Proxies
comment: An R implementation of SCOUT is available at this https URL
summary: Modern observational biomedical datasets contain increasingly extensive baseline and outcome measurements, yet detecting a clinically meaningful treatment effect remains difficult because investigators must identify an outcome that captures treatment response while adjusting for confounding distributed across numerous noisy baseline variables. We introduce SCOUT (Score-based Causal Outcome Learning Using Treatment signals), a framework that learns a clinically interpretable, treatment-responsive outcome while adjusting for confounding throughout the learning process. SCOUT constructs low-dimensional adjustment representations of high-dimensional baseline measurements to estimate the average treatment effect (ATE) and conditional average treatment effect (CATE) for the learned outcome. Importantly, the final adjustment space is at most two-dimensional, allowing treatment-effect heterogeneity to be estimated in this space rather than in the full high-dimensional covariate space. SCOUT also introduces a fourth-order statistic for testing treatment-effect heterogeneity that emphasizes unusually large deviations from the ATE. In synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments, the algorithm achieved competitive ATE estimation accuracy and substantially lower CATE estimation error. In an observational study of patients with bipolar disorder, SCOUT identified a clinically recognizable lithium-associated adverse-effect profile, detecting both a significant ATE (Holm-adjusted $p$ = 0.0026) and significant treatment-effect heterogeneity (Holm-adjusted $p$ = 0.033).These results demonstrate how jointly learning outcomes and controlling for confounding can facilitate the discovery of treatment effects in high-dimensional observational data.

AI.tldr: SCOUT learns a clinically interpretable, treatment-responsive outcome while adjusting for confounding, and it compresses baseline covariates into an adjustment space of at most two dimensions. It estimates the ATE and CATE and tests heterogeneity with a fourth-order statistic.
AI.motivation: In observational biomedical data with many noisy baseline and outcome variables, it is difficult to identify an outcome that captures treatment response while adjusting for confounding.
AI.method: Low-dimensional adjustment representations of high-dimensional baseline measurements are learned jointly with the outcome. Treatment-effect heterogeneity is estimated in the final two-dimensional space, and a fourth-order statistic that emphasizes unusually large deviations from the ATE is used to test heterogeneity.
AI.result: In synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments, SCOUT gives competitive ATE accuracy and substantially lower CATE error. In an observational study of bipolar disorder patients it identifies a clinically recognizable lithium-associated adverse-effect profile, with a significant ATE (Holm-adjusted p = 0.0026) and significant heterogeneity (Holm-adjusted p = 0.033).
AI.conclusion: Jointly learning the outcome and controlling for confounding can help discover treatment effects in high-dimensional observational data.

title: JUBILEE: A Benchmark Environment for Off-Policy Evaluation in Debt Collections
comment: 28 pages, 3 figures, 35 tables. Code: this https URL. Data: this https URL
summary: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates the value a candidate decision policy would achieve, using only data logged by the policy already in production. In debt collections, unrecorded factors can influence both actions and outcomes. This paper presents JUBILEE, a benchmark environment built around a debt-collections simulator that generates million-loan panels with competing risks, rare recovery events, and hidden factors driving both outcomes and assignment. The evaluation includes an 80-run comparison of tabular and gradient-boosted estimators under two synthetic outcome mechanisms and a 190-run parameter grid. Independent policy simulations provide reference values with estimated Monte Carlo uncertainty for a synthetic reward score and for simulated cash. With hidden factors influencing action assignment, several tabular methods agree closely while underestimating the field-visit policy's score, an error that also appears with boosted models. Intervals from tabular doubly robust estimation usually contain the reference without hidden assignment dependence but mostly miss it when that dependence is present. Estimates from randomized decisions do not show the same large error, although their limited precision leaves policy choice uncertain. The decision consequences depend on how policy value is defined. The field-visit policy ranks last under the score and first under simulated cash, which excludes channel costs. Under cash, log-based estimators miss this best candidate in nearly every run with hidden assignment dependence in the paired study. JUBILEE supports reproducible study of these failure modes under specified collections mechanisms.

AI.tldr: JUBILEE is a benchmark environment for off-policy evaluation in debt collections, built on a simulator with million-loan panels, competing risks, rare recoveries and hidden factors. It shows that log-based estimators can miss the best policy, depending on how policy value is defined.
AI.motivation: Off-policy evaluation in debt collections is hard because unrecorded factors influence both actions and outcomes, and existing evaluation practice lacks a reproducible testbed for these failure modes.
AI.method: A debt-collections simulator generates loan panels with competing risks and hidden factors. The study compares tabular and gradient-boosted estimators in an 80-run comparison under two synthetic outcome mechanisms and a 190-run parameter grid, with independent policy simulations as reference values.
AI.result: With hidden factors influencing assignment, several tabular methods underestimate the field-visit policy's score, and boosted models show the same error. Tabular doubly robust intervals usually cover the reference without hidden dependence but mostly miss it with dependence. Randomized decisions avoid the large error but have limited precision. The field-visit policy ranks last under the score and first under simulated cash, and under cash log-based estimators miss this policy in nearly every run with hidden dependence.
AI.conclusion: The ranking of policies depends on how value is defined, and the benchmark supports reproducible study of these OPE failure modes under specified collections mechanisms.

title: Toward a theory of Evaluability
summary: Machine learning models, particularly large foundation models, are increasingly evaluated along multiple axes that are relevant for their usage. In addition to accuracy measures appropriate for the specific task of interest, measures capturing safety, calibration and fairness properties are often of interest. The classical approach to these problems assumes that the test set has been held out from the training process, an assumption that is increasingly harder to justify for large foundation models. In this work, we formalize a notion of evaluability without this assumption, and ask if it is feasible to evaluate black-box models in settings where our test samples may have been used during training. We study this problem under different settings, capturing different levels of access to the model. We first study the natural setting, where the evaluator only looks at the output of the model on the test set. We fully characterize the class of distributions where accurate evaluation is possible, and show tight upper and lower bounds on the sample complexity of evaluation. Our results show that black-box evaluation in this setup is feasible if and only if the distribution is close to being small support. We then consider evaluation algorithms that can query the model on additional inputs and demonstrate connections to self-correctors studied in program testing. Using these, we show that a small amount of query access can increase the power of the evaluator for natural distributions and concept classes.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes evaluability, the feasibility of evaluating black-box models whose test samples may have appeared in training. It characterizes when accurate evaluation is possible and relates query access to self-correctors from program testing.
AI.motivation: The classical held-out test assumption is increasingly hard to justify for large foundation models, which are evaluated on axes such as safety, calibration and fairness.
AI.method: The authors study evaluation under different access levels. In the setting where the evaluator observes only model outputs on the test set, they characterize the distributions where evaluation is possible and derive tight sample complexity bounds. They then consider algorithms that can query the model on additional inputs and connect them to self-correctors.
AI.result: Black-box evaluation from test outputs alone is feasible if and only if the distribution is close to having small support. With a small amount of query access, the evaluator's power increases for natural distributions and concept classes.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation without a held-out assumption is possible only under restrictive conditions in the output-only setting, but limited query access substantially extends what can be evaluated.

title: Does Predictive Performance Translate to Causal Performance? Evaluating tabular foundation models as nuisance learners for causal effect estimation
summary: Tabular foundation models based on prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) achieve strong predictive performance, but their value for causal inference is unclear. We evaluated whether PFNs, which predict through in-context learning, could match or outperform conventional nuisance learners in supporting accurate causal estimation and reliable uncertainty quantification (inference). Learners modeled propensity scores and outcome regressions within doubly robust estimators of average causal effects, with and without cross-fitting, across synthetic and semi-synthetic settings with varying confounding complexity and effect heterogeneity. Under simple parametric data-generating processes, the PFNs were competitive with correctly specified parametric regressions and ensembles containing them. In more complex settings, they outperformed all conventional learners evaluated, including richly specified Super Learner ensembles, for both accuracy and uncertainty quantification. As sample size increased, only the two PFN models (TabPFN and Mitra) consistently approached nominal confidence interval coverage, whereas under-coverage persisted for conventional learners. In some settings, PFNs achieved near-nominal coverage and well-calibrated standard errors even without cross-fitting. At the smallest sample size (n=200) and in the higher-dimensional semi-synthetic settings, PFNs and other flexible learners exhibited poor coverage without cross-fitting. For PFNs, this appeared to be driven by propensity score overfitting consistent with in-sample memorization of treatment labels. These findings highlight the promise of prior-data fitted networks as in-context nuisance learners for causal estimation, while underscoring the need for further evaluation in challenging settings.

AI.tldr: The study evaluates tabular foundation models based on prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) as nuisance learners in doubly robust estimation of average causal effects. PFNs, TabPFN and Mitra in particular, often match or beat conventional learners, and only they approach nominal coverage as sample size grows.
AI.motivation: Tabular PFNs achieve strong predictive performance, but their value for causal inference, including reliable uncertainty quantification, was unclear.
